patch.value: Merge and rebase refuse to run when any untracked file exists, which is every real working tree

Found by driving the engine end to end against a real project rather than through its tests. In a scratch repository with pm-vcs installed as an extension, vcs init, add and commit all work, two branches were created and committed on, and vcs merge then refused with dirty_worktree: the working tree has changes that are not committed, merging would mix them into the result.

The working tree had no uncommitted changes. vcs status --json reported staged 0, unstaged 0, untracked 682. Every one of the 682 was a file the repository had never tracked — the pm extension install artifacts under .agents/pm/extensions, pm's own schema files, .gitignore and .gitattributes. Nothing that a merge could mix into anything.

The cause is a single definition. engine/worktree.ts computes clean as staged, unstaged and untracked all being empty, and both merge and rebase gate on that one flag. Folding untracked into cleanliness is right for a question like is this tree fully captured; it is wrong as a merge precondition, because an untracked file is by definition not part of any tree being merged and cannot be mixed into the result.

The consequence is that merge is unusable in any real project. Every working tree has untracked files: build output, node_modules, editor state, a scratch file. A version control system whose merge cannot run in the presence of an untracked file cannot be used for the concurrent-agent workflow this package exists to support, and the failure message names the wrong cause, so a user is sent looking for uncommitted work that does not exist.

Git's rule is the one to adopt and it is narrower than either extreme: a merge runs with untracked files present, and refuses only when it would need to write to a path that is currently untracked, because that specific case would destroy unversioned content.

merge and rebase run when the working tree has untracked files and no staged or unstaged changes; both still refuse when tracked files are modified; both refuse when the incoming tree would write to a currently untracked path, and the message names that path rather than reporting a generic dirty tree; the clean flag on status keeps its present meaning for callers that want it; and a test drives the real engine through the sequence that found this rather than asserting on the flag

value.text:
Found by installing this package as an extension into a scratch project and driving it end to end with real files, not through its own tests. vcs init, add and commit worked, two branches were created and committed on, and vcs merge then refused with dirty_worktree while vcs status --json reported staged 0, unstaged 0, untracked 682. Every one of the 682 was a pm extension artifact, a schema file, .gitignore or .gitattributes — files the repository had never tracked and that no merge could mix into anything.

The fix adopts git's rule, which is narrower than either extreme. Uncommitted changes to tracked files still refuse, because that work is in no tree and would be mixed into the result. Untracked files no longer refuse on their own. An untracked file refuses only when the incoming tree names that same path, because materializing it would destroy content no commit records — and the refusal names the colliding paths, because a generic dirty-tree message sends the reader looking for uncommitted work that does not exist.

Two details chosen deliberately. The refusal reports every colliding path rather than the first, so one round of cleanup can clear them all, and caps the list at ten with a count of the remainder, because a wholly untracked checkout of the incoming tree would otherwise produce an unreadable error. The clean flag on status keeps its existing meaning for callers that want to ask whether the tree is fully captured; what changed is that merge and history rewriting no longer use that question to answer a different one.

Verified against the original failure rather than only in tests: the same scratch project, the same two branches, now merges cleanly. Both agents' work is present — agent A's parseStrict in parser.ts and agent B's serializer.ts — the commit has two parents, and vcs verify reports 15 objects verified.

Regression tests proved non-vacuous by reverting the fix: two of the three fail. The third, which asserts that a modified tracked file still refuses, passes against both implementations by design — it guards the over-correction, not the fix, and a test that fails in both directions would mean the fix had gone too far.

value.note: merge runs with untracked files present, and refuses only when one would be overwritten

value.note: merge refuses when the incoming tree would overwrite an untracked path, and names it

patch.value: Replaced the clean-flag precondition with git's rule: tracked changes refuse, untracked files do not, and an untracked path refuses only when the incoming tree would overwrite it.
A merge runs in a working tree carrying untracked build output or dependencies, still refuses on modified tracked files, and refuses with a named path when it would destroy unversioned content.

The originally failing scratch merge succeeds with both agents' work present, two parents, and vcs verify reporting 15 objects verified. Coverage holds at 100/100/100/100 across all files including repo.ts.

merge and rebase now gate on uncommitted tracked changes rather than on any untracked file, and refuse an untracked path only when the incoming tree names it, naming the collisions. The scratch project that found this now merges cleanly with both branches' work present.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Two review findings, both consequences of this change rather than pre-existing, and one of them critical. Both are fixed.

The critical one: the overwrite guard compared exact paths only, so an untracked dir/local.txt against an incoming tree holding dir as a file slipped through, and the mirror case did too. Because advanceHead runs before materializeTree, the write then failed with ENOTDIR or EISDIR after the ref had already moved — leaving HEAD naming a tree the index and working tree do not hold, which the code's own comment calls the one state this engine promises never to produce. Collision detection now covers both directions: an untracked path under something the incoming tree holds as a file, and an incoming path under something the working tree holds as an untracked file.

The second: relaxing assertCleanWorktree to ignore untracked paths made merge usable and simultaneously left cherryPick and revert able to destroy an untracked file, because those two advance the ref before materializing and were relying on the strict check to keep the tree empty. The collision guard is now a separate assertion precisely so it can run at the right moment for each command — merge can check up front, while cherry-pick and revert only know the resulting tree after planning and must check between planning and advanceHead.

That separation is the general lesson worth recording. Relaxing a precondition is never local: every caller that was relying on the strict version inherits the relaxation silently, and here two of them advanced a ref on the strength of a guarantee that had quietly been withdrawn.

All three regression tests were proved non-vacuous by reverting to exact-path matching and removing the two command guards: all three fail. Coverage holds at 100 percent lines, branches and functions across all files including repo.ts, and the docstring gate reports 39 files with 214 declarations documented.

patch.value: The originally failing scratch merge succeeds with both branches' work present and verify reporting 15 objects. All three collision regressions fail when the guard is reverted. Coverage 100/100/100/100 across all files including repo.ts.

Merge runs with untracked build output present; a directory/file collision in either direction refuses; and cherry-pick and revert refuse before advancing the ref rather than failing with an errno after it.

Replaced the clean-flag precondition with git's rule, and made the collision guard a separate assertion each command runs at the moment it knows its resulting tree, so a ref never advances on a tree the working tree cannot accept.
merge, rebase, cherry-pick and revert now run with untracked files present and refuse only a real collision, detected in both directions and before any ref advances.
